\begin{abstract}
Compute-governance regimes that restrict large training runs presuppose that a
regulator can tell when training happens on monitored hardware, and a power
meter outside the operator's control is the one passive channel available
against an operator who does not cooperate. We ask what such a meter can certify,
and answer with a ladder of four claims, each with a stated information cost
and a hard ceiling. Evidence comes from a literature-parameterized scenario
model of datacentre AI workloads and an explicit off-chip observation model,
against both a benign operator and a concealing one who knows the detector. The
iteration cadence of synchronous training is recoverable by a tracked
cyclostationary detector, but the complete pipeline admits no analytic
calibration, so we report it as an effective score with per-trace surrogate
calibration rather than a constant false-alarm-rate test. Our central result
is the de-periodicisation frontier, which prices hiding against measured
throughput anchors and is strongly asymmetric: varying real work per iteration
hides from every fixed-frequency test at essentially zero cost, while the
tracking class holds until that variation is extreme, where it still detects
about half of runs. That extreme level is also free in throughput, so its price,
if any, lies in learning efficiency, which we do not measure. Two limits are firmer than the detectors. The observation channel is
itself a condition on every claim --- a one-second-integrating, one-hertz
meter defeats all detectors on an honest workload --- and the meter certifies
a physical schedule, not training semantics: five non-training loads,
including one computing gradients and discarding them, are classified as
training by every rule we test. Escaping that ceiling means leaving the
passive channel for an active challenge protocol, which we specify but do not
run.
\end{abstract}

% ============================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
% ============================================================================

% ---------- [1] HOOK: the concrete governance problem and the one passive channel ----------
AI governance agreements will require regulating training runs \citep{shavit2023chinchilla,sastry2024computing,baker2025verifying,heim2024thresholds}. This will require an external verifier to identify when training is occurring on a monitored cluster, against an operator who is trying to hide their training. There are multiple channels that could provide the verifier with diagnostic information to identify hidden training. These include on-chip mechanisms that log activities for later analysis, network taps that monitor data exchanged between chips, or human-centred approaches such as whistleblower programs or interviews of operator personnel. However each of these channels requires trusting either hardware that is under the control of the operator, or the operator personnel themselves. Conversely, off-chip sensors that take analog, physical measurements of the cluster (e.g. power or electromagnetic emissions) do not require trusting the operator. Such sensors could be retrofitted to existing datacentres (e.g. clamping a power meter on an input cable) and secured against tampering by the operator. 


% ---------- [2a] LITERATURE: what is established about the physical signature ----------
AI training has already been shown to leave a signature in the power drawn by the hardware that can serve as a diagnostic to identify and separate training from inference. A $10$\,MHz current probe clamped around the GPU's PCIe power supply cables can separate training from
inference and from non-AI work at $97\%$ accuracy \citep{gargiulo2026workload}, a result robust against many but not all adversarial strategies. On-chip $1$\,Hz telemetry counters that measure power (among other telemetry: utilisation, memory, etc.) can classify training at $95\%$ accuracy, again a result robust against many but not all adversarial strategies \citep{rahman2026telemetry}. In practice, any realistic AI governance agreements that use off-chip sensors will rarely have such fine-grained access to the GPU hardware. Power meters that can be retrofitted to existing facilities and secured against tampering are likely to sit at the level of the rack or facility input, with sampling frequencies ${\sim}10$\,Hz (i.e. three to four orders of magnitude slower than the board probe) and behind a power-delivery path that low-passes and dilutes the signal. At this level training can be identified and it is large enough that datacentre and grid operators treat it as an engineering control problem to be dealt with~\citep{patel2023polca,ko2025widearea}. 

% ---------- [4] THE AIM: what this paper does, as refutable claims with pointers ----------
In this paper we develop a new method for detecting training signatures given noisy facility level power measurements, against an adversarial operator who is trying to hide their training. 


%to be done once the paper scrop/strucutre is better established
We do:

* specify anoff-chip observation model and a literature-parameterised generator of
datacentre training and inference power, 

* construct a detector  a detector for the cadence that tracks the wandering line, borrowing thehcniqus ffrom signal analysis and GW astrophysics

* We construct the Pareto frontier and show the trade-off between how much of the cadence an concealing operator removes and
what that removal costs in measured throughput, and derive an identifiability
lower bound on the cost of hiding to a stated detectability
(\cref{sec:frontier,subsec:costbound}). 

*We derive a minimum meter specification, the sampling rate, integration time and in-band
transfer i.e. the specs needed for a meter to work 



* We restrict attention to synchronous, iteration-structured
training observed through a time-resolved trace; the integrated-energy channel,
asynchronous schedules and the calibration of the generator to distributed
hardware are outside scope, and \cref{sec:reality,sec:discussion} say what that
costs.



 Unlike a covert transmitter, a training operator cannot freely reshape its signal: the communication phase has a fixed physical duration, and every distortion of the cadence costs throughput. It is this constraint that makes a cost-of-hiding bound possible.



% ---------- [5] ROADMAP ----------
This paper is organised as follows. \Cref{sec:scenario} gives the model of
datacentre training and inference power that generates every trace below, and
\cref{sec:threat} fixes what the verifier sees through an off-chip meter and
what a concealing operator may do to hide from it. \Cref{sec:methods} develops the
detector, a Viterbi line tracker; \cref{sec:results} reports its power against
the inference null and the minimum meter it needs; and \cref{sec:frontier}
prices what it costs a concealing operator to defeat it. \Cref{sec:discussion}
states what a detection does and does not certify, holds the model against
measured single-GPU hardware, and reads the results back as a ladder of claims
a regulator can buy.


\section{A model of datacentre training power}
\label{sec:scenario}
% ============================================================================
In this section we build a model of the power draw from a data centre running AI workloads. This model will serve as a synthetic data generator to test our methods, in lieu of having access to real empirical data. We adopt the stochastic model of AI training power from \citet{ko2025widearea}, developed for the analysis of grid stability, modified to add an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck drift on the training frequency. The reader is referred to \citet{ko2025widearea} for the full training model and its context.

This section is organised as follows. \Cref{subsec:ko} describes the power draw from a
training workload, following \citet{ko2025widearea}, and adds our drift of its cadence.
\Cref{subsec:finetune} describes the power draw from a fine-tuning workload. \Cref{subsec:null} describes the power draw from an inference workload. \Cref{subsec:aggregate} combines these workloads into the load of a whole
datacentre: one dominant workload, either training or inference, over a
background of smaller trainings and fine-tunings. \Cref{tab:params} collects
every parameter value of the model. 

\subsection{Training}
\label{subsec:ko}

Multi GPU AI training of the kind that typifies frontier models is composed of a two-phase iterative cycle. First there is a power intensive, high compute ``up" phase where the forward/backward pass happens. Second there is a low power, low compute, communication ``down" phase where the gradient all reduce happens. 

Iteration $i$ has period
\begin{equation}
	T_i \;=\; \frac{1}{f_0\,(1+\xi_i)}, \qquad \xi_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_\xi^2),
	\label{eq:period}
\end{equation}
where $f_0$ is the baseline fluctuation frequency. For a given training run $f_0$ is fixed. Between training runs $f_0$ can vary depending on model size, batch size, parallelism layout, interconnect and hardware \citep{patel2024characterizing,jain2024pal}. To describe the inter-workload variation, we take  $f_0 \sim \mathcal{U}(f^{\mathrm{lo}}, f^{\mathrm{hi}})$ . The period splits into an up-phase of duration
$\rho_i T_i$ and a down-phase of duration $(1-\rho_i) T_i$, with the phase ratio
$\rho_i \sim \mathcal{U}(\rho^{\mathrm{lo}}, \rho^{\mathrm{hi}})$ redrawn each iteration. Writing $t$ for time
within iteration $i$, $P(t)$ for the power the run draws above the facility's static
overhead (added in \cref{subsec:obsmap}), and $P_{\mathrm{peak}}$ for its peak,
\begin{equation}
	\frac{P(t)}{P_{\mathrm{peak}}} =
	\begin{cases}
		1 + \Delta^{\mathrm{up}}_i + \nu^{\mathrm{up}}(t), & t < \rho_i T_i,\\[2pt]
		1 - \Delta^{\mathrm{dn}}_i + \nu^{\mathrm{dn}}(t), & t \geq \rho_i T_i,
	\end{cases}
	\label{eq:ko}
\end{equation}
where the per-phase level offsets are
$\Delta^{\mathrm{up}}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_\Delta^2)$ and
$\Delta^{\mathrm{dn}}_i \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu_\Delta, \sigma_\Delta^2)$, and
$\nu^{\mathrm{up}}$, $\nu^{\mathrm{dn}}$ are zero-mean intra-phase Gaussian
fluctuations with standard deviations $\kappa_\nu s^{\mathrm{up}}_i$ and
$\kappa_\nu s^{\mathrm{dn}}_i$. The $s^{\mathrm{up}}_i$ and $s^{\mathrm{dn}}_i$
are redrawn each phase, uniformly from the ranges
$[s^{\mathrm{up,lo}}, s^{\mathrm{up,hi}}]$ and
$[s^{\mathrm{dn,lo}}, s^{\mathrm{dn,hi}}]$, and $\kappa_\nu$ is a fixed
scale factor. \Cref{tab:params} lists the values
of every parameter in this section.

\Cref{eq:period,eq:ko} are the exact training workload model from \citet{ko2025widearea}. We make one modification, adding a slow drift to the cadence $f_0$ itself. The jitter $\xi_i$ does not produce drift. Because it is redrawn independently
each iteration, the cadence averaged over many iterations is still $f_0$. The
timing errors accumulate as a random walk in phase, which broadens the spectral
line into a Lorentzian of full width $\approx 2\pi\sigma_\xi^2 f_0$ (to leading
order in $\sigma_\xi$) but leaves its centre at $f_0$. Real runs vary differently. Specifically, the iteration time changes in ways that persist.
Every training step waits for the slowest GPU, so one slow component slows the
whole run. In a production LLM cluster, these slowdowns last for the whole job
rather than varying from step to step \citep{lin2025stragglers}. Hardware can
also keep running but degrade: CPU contention, overheating GPUs and congested
network links cut throughput by tens of percent for periods of tens of seconds
to hours \citep{wu2024falcon}. Over a day,
temperature shifts throughput by a further $1$--$2\%$
\citep{grattafiori2024llama3}. 

We model this by letting the cadence of iteration $i$ be $f_0 g_i$, where $g_i$
is a discrete Ornstein--Uhlenbeck (first-order autoregressive) process that
starts at $g_0 = 1$ and reverts to $1$:
\begin{equation}
	g_i - 1 \;=\; (1-\theta)\,(g_{i-1} - 1) \;+\; \epsilon_i,
	\qquad \epsilon_i \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_g^2).
	\label{eq:ou}
\end{equation}
The period of \cref{eq:period} becomes
\begin{equation}
	T_i \;=\; \frac{1}{f_0\, g_i\,(1+\xi_i)},
	\label{eq:period_drift}
\end{equation}
which reduces to \cref{eq:period} when $g_i \equiv 1$. The stationary variance
of \cref{eq:ou} is $\sigma_g^2/(2\theta - \theta^2)$, so we set
\begin{equation}
	\sigma_g \;=\; \frac{\sigma_f}{f_0}\sqrt{2\theta - \theta^2},
	\label{eq:ou_sigma}
\end{equation}
which makes the stationary standard deviation of the instantaneous cadence
$f_0 g_i$ equal to $\sigma_f$, in Hz. The autocorrelation of $g_i$ at lag $k$
is $(1-\theta)^k$, so the cadence stays correlated over  $\sim 1/\theta$
iterations. Over that span it wanders by $\sigma_f$, which can exceed both the
line width set by $\xi_i$ and the frequency resolution of a trace. We clip
$g_i$ from below at $g_{\min}$ so the period stays finite. We hold $\theta$ fixed and treat $\sigma_f$ as a free
parameter, sweeping it in \cref{sec:results}.



\subsection{Fine-tuning}
\label{subsec:finetune}
Fine-tuning workloads can be represented using the same structure as in Section \ref{subsec:ko}, with different parameters (\cref{tab:params}). We denote the fine-tuning frequency as $f_1$. Compared with training, it has a lower cadence
band, a longer tail phase (larger $\rho_i$), a deeper tail-to-idle swing (larger
$\mu_\Delta$), and slightly smaller level offsets and intra-phase noise.
We apply the cadence drift of \cref{eq:ou} only to the dominant run;
fine-tuning and background training runs keep a fixed cadence ($\sigma_f = 0$).

\subsection{Inference}
\label{subsec:null}
\citet{ko2025widearea} do not present a model for power draw of inference workloads. We now construct one. We superpose three structures on a constant mean serving power load $B$. First, token generation (decode). Serving systems use continuous batching,
which adds and removes requests from the batch at every step
\citep{yu2022orca,kwon2023vllm}. A per-step cadence exists, but the batch
composition reshuffles every step. Unlike training, there is therefore no
characteristic frequency: decode power smears across a broad band with no
coherent frequency path. We model it as band-limited noise $b(t)$ of unit RMS
over $[f_b^{\mathrm{lo}}, f_b^{\mathrm{hi}}]$, scaled by an amplitude $A$. Second, expert-load imbalance. Under sparse mixture-of-experts routing, tokens
are not spread evenly across the experts \citep{shazeer2017moe}, so the work per
step varies with the mix of requests. We model this as a slow envelope on the
decode power: a unit-variance Ornstein--Uhlenbeck process $u(t)$ with
correlation time $\tau_u$, entering at depth $m$. Amplitude modulation spreads
the decode energy into sidebands, which makes the null harder, not easier. Third, prompt processing (prefill). Each request begins with a prompt phase that
is brief, compute-bound, and draws more power than token generation
\citep{patel2024characterizing,patel2024splitwise}. We model these phases as box
pulses $s(\cdot)$ of duration $d_p$ and height $a$, arriving at times $\tau_k$
from a Poisson process of rate $\lambda_p$. These memoryless arrivals carry no
line and simply raise the broadband in-band level. Together,
\begin{equation}
	\frac{P^{\mathrm{inf}}(t)}{P_{\mathrm{peak}}} \;=\;
	B \;+\; A\,\bigl[1 + m\,u(t)\bigr]\,b(t) \;+\; \sum_k a\,s(t - \tau_k).
	\label{eq:null}
\end{equation}
The forms of these structures follow how LLM serving systems schedule work;
their amplitudes are our choice (\cref{tab:params}). We set them so that
inference is a loud confound rather than a quiet one. As
\cref{fig:scenario_traces} shows, it delivers more in-band power than training
but an order of magnitude less spectral contrast.





\subsection{Aggregate}
\label{subsec:aggregate}
A datacentre rarely runs one job at a time. Following \citet{ko2025widearea} we write the load behind a single meter as the aggregate of one dominant training run over a background of
smaller trainings and fine-tunings,
\begin{equation}
	P_{\mathrm{AI}}(t) \;=\; P^{\mathrm{main}}(t)
	\;+\; \sum_{j=1}^{N_{\mathrm{tr}}} P^{\mathrm{tr}}_j(t)
	\;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{ft}}} P^{\mathrm{ft}}_k(t).
	\label{eq:aggregate}
\end{equation}
where $P^{\mathrm{main}}$ is the power of the dominant training run,
$P^{\mathrm{tr}}_j$ that of the $j$-th of $N_{\mathrm{tr}}$ smaller training
runs, and $P^{\mathrm{ft}}_k$ that of the $k$-th of $N_{\mathrm{ft}}$
fine-tuning runs. Each term is an independent draw of \cref{eq:ko}, with its own
cadence, phase ratios, and level offsets. $P^{\mathrm{main}}$ and the
$P^{\mathrm{tr}}_j$ use the training parameters and the $P^{\mathrm{ft}}_k$ use
the fine-tuning parameters; only $P^{\mathrm{main}}$ carries the cadence drift
of \cref{eq:ou}. Peak power is split between the dominant run, the small
trainings, and the fine-tunings in the ratio
$w_{\mathrm{main}} : w_{\mathrm{tr}} : w_{\mathrm{ft}}$, and each background
share is divided equally among its members. Each small training draws its cadence from the same
band as the dominant run, so the background carries weak lines of its own
inside the search band.

We define the null aggregate as the same datacentre with the dominant training
run replaced by inference (\cref{subsec:null}). The background is unchanged,
\begin{equation}
	P^{\mathrm{null}}_{\mathrm{AI}}(t) \;=\; P^{\mathrm{inf}}(t)
	\;+\; \sum_{j=1}^{N_{\mathrm{tr}}} P^{\mathrm{tr}}_j(t)
	\;+\; \sum_{k=1}^{N_{\mathrm{ft}}} P^{\mathrm{ft}}_k(t),
	\label{eq:aggregate_null}
\end{equation}
with $P^{\mathrm{inf}}$ from \cref{eq:null} at the same
share $w_{\mathrm{main}}$. The two aggregate classes are then power-matched and
both contain the background's weak lines. \Cref{fig:scenario_traces} shows the four resulting workload classes as
a verifier would see them.

% ============================================================================
\section{Measurement and threat model}
\label{sec:threat}
% ============================================================================

This section specifies how the power drawn by the data centre reaches the verifier (i.e. the measurement model), and what the facility operator can control (i.e. the threat model). The verifier wants to know whether a monitored facility is running undeclared training. We frame this as a hypothesis test. Under the null hypothesis $\mathcal{H}_0$ the facility runs its declared workload, which for a monitored cluster is dominated by inference: the inference model of \cref{subsec:null}, alone or
over the background of \cref{eq:aggregate_null}. Under the alternative hypothesis $\mathcal{H}_1$ a training run of \cref{subsec:ko} takes the place of that inference, alone or over the same background (\cref{eq:aggregate}). \Cref{subsec:channel} outlines the channel through which either hypothesis reaches the verifier. \Cref{subsec:adversary} outlines who controls the load, what they know, and what
they may change. 

\subsection{The measurement model}
\label{subsec:channel}
\label{subsec:obsmap}

\Cref{sec:scenario} gives the power $P_{\mathrm{AI}}(t)$ drawn by the AI
workload above the facility's static overhead, in units of
$P_{\mathrm{peak}}$. The total power behind the meter is
\begin{equation}
	P_{\mathrm{fac}}(t) \;=\; P_0 + P_{\mathrm{AI}}(t),
	\label{eq:fac}
\end{equation}
with $P_{\mathrm{AI}}$ given by \cref{eq:aggregate} under $\mathcal{H}_1$, by
\cref{eq:aggregate_null} under $\mathcal{H}_0$, or by a single workload of
\cref{sec:scenario} when a result drops the background. The verifier holds one scalar time series from a meter outside the operator's
control. The meter reads
\begin{equation}
	\begin{gathered}
		P_{\mathrm{meter}}[n] \;=\; (h * P_{\mathrm{fac}})(t_n) + \eta[n],\\
		t_n = n/f_s, \qquad h \;=\; h_{\mathrm{ins}} * h_{\mathrm{del}}.
	\end{gathered}
	\label{eq:meter}
\end{equation}
The meter filters the facility power, samples it at rate $f_s$, and adds
interference and measurement noise $\eta[n]$ on its own sample grid. Round
brackets denote continuous time and square brackets index the meter's
samples.The filter is a linear time-invariant system with impulse response $h$, which has
two parts. The delivery path $h_{\mathrm{del}}$ is everything between the
accelerators and the meter: power supplies, distribution, and any conversion
or storage. The instrument $h_{\mathrm{ins}}$ is the meter's own filtering:
its integration window and calibration gain.  \Cref{fig:power_chain} traces
the power from the workloads to the verifier.
\begin{figure*}[t]
	\centering
	\resizebox{\linewidth}{!}{\input{fig_power_chain}}
	\caption{The measurement chain. The workloads of \cref{sec:scenario} and a
	static overhead sum to the facility power $P_{\mathrm{fac}}$
	(\cref{eq:fac}), which passes through the delivery path and the meter
	before additive terms are added (\cref{eq:meter}). Sketches show one
	training cadence as it is smoothed, sampled, and made noisy; they are
	illustrative. Everything left of the dashed line is under the operator's
	control (\cref{subsec:adversary}). Red labels mark where the adversarial
	strategies of \cref{tab:attacks} act. $\eta$ lumps instrument noise with
	interference that physically originates behind the meter, such as the
	power-controller line. In the nominal channel the delivery path
	passes the power through unchanged ($h_{\mathrm{del}} = \delta$) and the meter samples at $20$\,Hz with no integration
	(\cref{tab:meter}).}
	\label{fig:power_chain}
\end{figure*}



Following \citet{ko2025widearea} we assume the delivery path passes the power
through unchanged, such that $h_{\mathrm{del}}$ is a delta function and
$h_{\mathrm{del}} * P_{\mathrm{fac}} = P_{\mathrm{fac}}$. The low-pass and
notch of \cref{tab:meter} relax this assumption in our sweeps. The notch
stands for an anti-resonance of the delivery network that happens to sit near
the cadence; it is the one stage that removes signal in-band while leaving the
rest of the spectrum intact.

The instrument $h_{\mathrm{ins}}$ is the meter's own response
(\cref{tab:meter}). We model it as a calibration gain $g$ followed by a
trailing boxcar, so that each reading is the mean power over the preceding
window $\tau$: $h_{\mathrm{ins}}(t) = g/\tau$ for $0 \le t < \tau$ and zero
otherwise. Its frequency response has magnitude
\begin{equation}
	\lvert H_{\mathrm{ins}}(f) \rvert \;=\; g\,
	\left\lvert \frac{\sin(\pi f \tau)}{\pi f \tau} \right\rvert,
	\label{eq:boxcar}
\end{equation}
which passes slow variations and attenuates fast ones, with a zero at every
multiple of $1/\tau$. A window longer than about $0.6$\,s puts the first zero
inside the $0.3$--$1.7$\,Hz search band, and a $1$\,s window puts it at the
band centre. In the nominal channel $g = 1$ and $\tau \to 0$, so
$h_{\mathrm{ins}}$ is also a delta function, and the meter samples at
$f_s = 20$\,Hz. Unlike the delivery path, the instrument is the verifier's to
choose, and \cref{subsec:meter_spec} asks what $\tau$ and $f_s$ must be for
detection to hold.

The additive term $\eta[n]$ collects everything that reaches the readings
without passing through $h$ (\cref{tab:meter}). In the nominal channel it is
white meter noise of $\sigma_\eta = 4$\,W. Two further terms are available: a
slowly wandering baseline, standing for a drifting operating point such as
cooling load, and a controller limit cycle, a square wave whose frequency
itself wanders, modelled on the power-management oscillation measured on an
A100 (\cref{sec:reality}). The controller is the first appearance of an
instrument line: a persistent, slowly wandering spectral line that the
facility's hardware produces with no training present.
\Cref{subsec:identifiability} returns to it.

Three numbers carry units. The peak power $P_{\mathrm{peak}} = 850$\,W and
overhead $P_0 = 250$\,W (\cref{tab:params}) are those of a single accelerator
board, and the meter noise $\sigma_\eta = 4$\,W is an illustrative choice,
about $0.5\%$ of the mean reading, not a measured value. None of the three is
critical. $P_0$ is constant, so it lies at zero frequency, outside the search
band. What sets detectability is the training line against everything else in
the band, and at the nominal setting that is dominated by the workloads
themselves: in the search band the inference null's power spectral density
exceeds that of the meter noise by about four orders of magnitude, and the
training trace's own off-line floor exceeds it by about three. Meter noise
binds only when it is raised far above $4$\,W, which
\cref{fig:scenario_meter} does over two decades.


Each trace lasts $T = 300$\,s, a frequency resolution of
$1/T \approx 3$\,mHz. In the nominal channel every stage of
\cref{tab:meter} is off except the white meter noise. With the noise also
off, the
map returns $P_{\mathrm{fac}}$ unchanged and consumes no randomness. Two limits apply. The linear time-invariant form of $h$ is a first
approximation; a real delivery path may be operating-point dependent. And the
model quantises only in time, through the integration window and the sample
grid; it has no amplitude quantisation. Until simultaneous on-device and
external-meter measurement is performed, claims about what reaches an
off-chip sensor are predictions (\cref{sec:reality}).

\Cref{fig:scenario_meter} shows how the channel attenuates the training
line. For a fixed training workload we vary one axis of \cref{tab:meter} at a
time and measure an effective signal-to-noise ratio at the cadence: the
spectral power at $f_0$ over the in-band power the meter itself adds,
relative to the nominal channel. Every axis lowers it, and two remove the line
entirely within the range a real meter might occupy: a $1$\,s integration
window, whose first zero falls at $1$\,Hz (\cref{eq:boxcar}), and a $1$\,Hz
sample rate. This concerns the signal reaching the verifier, not any
detector; what each detector does with what survives, and hence the minimum
meter specification, is \cref{subsec:meter_spec}.

\subsection{The threat model}
\label{subsec:adversary}

%\paragraph{Parties and trust.} 
The verifier installs and owns the power meter.
The meter is tamper-evident, the verifier chooses its specification, and the
operator cannot forge the meter noise $\eta$. The operator controls everything behind the meter, e.g. which jobs run, how they
are scheduled, what else shares the facility, and the power-delivery path
itself. Energy storage or
power smoothing between the accelerators and the meter can low-pass or notch
the load, and datacentre and grid operators already treat smoothing training
load as an engineering problem \citep{ko2025widearea}. We represent partial
smoothing by the filtering stages of \cref{tab:meter}, and
\cref{subsec:meter_spec} asks how much of it the verifier can tolerate. A
store large enough to flatten the load entirely would erase any passive
signature; we do not model it, and discuss it among the limitations
(\cref{subsec:scope}). The operator knows the
detector, its parameters, its threshold, and the meter specification. It does
not know the realisation of $\eta$. %Kerckhoffs' principle

%\paragraph{Three operators.} 
We consider three types of facility operator. First a \emph{compliant} operator runs only its declared inference. A \emph{benign} operator trains without regard to being caught by the power meter.  A \emph{concealing} operator trains, knows the detector, and reshapes its workload to try to evade it. The concealing operator's objective is to train
without the being detected by the verifier. They use different adversarial strategies to try to subvert the verifier's detection. \Cref{tab:attacks} lists the adversarial strategies considered in this work. They
fall into five categories: disturbing the timing of iterations, relocating the
cadence, reshaping the power waveform within an iteration, mixing the run with
other load, and degrading the channel. In principle the strategies may be composed, but we treat them individually. Adversarial strategies have a cost to the operator in terms of training throughput. Each strategy therefore trades concealment against cost.

%\paragraph{Out of scope.} 
Three things lie outside this threat model. First, the
operator does not tamper with the meter or forge its noise. Second tt does not run a
semantic decoy, that is a load that reproduces the physical schedule of
training without training,  since manufacturing evidence of the activity it
is hiding buys a concealing operator nothing. Finally, it does not
move the training cadence outside the searched band or abandon synchronous iteration
altogether; both are scope restrictions on the population we target
(\cref{subsec:scope}). 

% ============================================================================
\section{Detection method}
\label{sec:methods}
% ============================================================================

In this section we present a detection method that ingests  $P_{\mathrm{meter}}[n]$, \cref{eq:meter}, and decides between $\mathcal{H}_0$ and $\mathcal{H}_1$ (\cref{sec:threat}). The two hypotheses are separated by the iteration cadence of synchronous training. Under $\mathcal{H}_1$ the two-phase cycle of the dominant run (\cref{eq:ko}) puts a strong, narrow spectral line at its cadence $f_0$. Under $\mathcal{H}_0$ the inference that replaces it spreads its power across the band with no line
(\cref{subsec:null}), and the only lines left are the background's weak ones
(\cref{subsec:aggregate}). A line at a fixed frequency has classical tests. But
the cadence of a real run wanders by $\sigma_f$ even without an adversary
(\cref{eq:ou}), and a concealing operator can make it wander further or vary
the work per iteration, which defeats a fixed-frequency test cheaply
(see \cref{sec:frontier}). The detector therefore has to follow the line as it
moves.

This section is organised as follows. \Cref{subsec:viterbi} defines the
detector, a Viterbi line tracker borrowed from passive sonar and
continuous-gravitational-wave searches. \Cref{subsec:threshold} sets the threshold at which the detector declares training.
\Cref{subsec:comparators} defines the two fixed-frequency tests we compare it
against.

\subsection{Viterbi line tracking}
\label{subsec:viterbi}

We follow the line with the hidden-Markov frequency tracking developed for
passive sonar \citep{streit1990frequency} and carried into
continuous-gravitational-wave searches
\citep{suvorova2016hmm,bayley2019soap,djurovic2011viterbi}. The tracker has
three parts: a spectrogram of the trace, a contrast map built from it, and a
search for the best slowly varying path through that map.

Let $x[n] = P_{\mathrm{meter}}[n] - \bar
P_{\mathrm{meter}}$ be the mean-removed meter trace, $N = f_s T$ samples long.
We cut it into frames of $M$ samples that overlap by half, a hop of $H = M/2$,
and take the power spectrum of each:
\begin{equation}
	S_{kj} \;=\; \Bigl\lvert \sum_{m=0}^{M-1} w[m]\,x[jH + m]\,
	e^{-2\pi i k m / M} \Bigr\rvert^2,
	\label{eq:spectrogram}
\end{equation}
for frames $j = 0, \dots, N_t - 1$, where $w$ is a tapered (Tukey) window and $N_t = \lfloor (N - M)/H \rfloor + 1$
is the number of frames. Bin $k$ sits at frequency $f_k = k f_s / M$. We
choose $M$ so that each frame lasts $M/f_s = 16$\,s, which gives bins
$\Delta f = 1/16 = 62.5$\,mHz wide, fine enough to resolve a line near $1$\,Hz,
while leaving many frames to track over: a $300$\,s trace gives $N_t = 36$
frames, $8$\,s apart. Only the bins with $f_k \in \mathcal{B}$ enter the
tracker, $23$ of them in the nominal channel. Every detector in this paper searches the band
$\mathcal{B} = [0.3, 1.7]$\,Hz. This is the training cadence band
$[f^{\mathrm{lo}}, f^{\mathrm{hi}}] = [0.5, 1.5]$\,Hz of \cref{tab:params},
widened by $0.2$\,Hz on each side so that a cadence drawn near either edge
stays in the band as it wanders.

We normalise each frame by its median over the band,
\begin{equation}
	L_{kj} \;=\; \ln S_{kj} \;-\; \ln \tilde S_j,
	\label{eq:contrast}
\end{equation}
where $\tilde S_j$ is the median of $S_{kj}$ over the in-band bins of frame
$j$. $L_{kj}$ measures how far bin $k$ stands above the typical in-band level of
its own frame. The normalisation keeps a slow change in overall power from masquerading as a line.

The hidden state is the frequency bin occupied by the
cadence in each frame. The prior that a real cadence wanders slowly enters as
a penalty $\lambda$ per bin of frequency change between consecutive frames. The
detection statistic is the score of the best path, averaged over frames,
\begin{equation}
	V \;=\; \frac{1}{N_t}\,\max_{k_0,\dots,k_{N_t-1}}
	\Biggl[\,\sum_{j=0}^{N_t-1} L_{k_j j}
	\;-\; \lambda \sum_{j=1}^{N_t-1} \lvert k_j - k_{j-1}\rvert\Biggr],
	\label{eq:viterbi}
\end{equation}
with $\lambda = 1$ throughout. A path pays one unit of log-contrast for each
$62.5$\,mHz step it takes between frames, so it can follow a drift of about
one bin per frame (about $8$\,mHz\,s$^{-1}$) if the line it follows is bright
enough to pay for it. Dynamic programming evaluates the maximum over all
$23^{N_t}$ paths exactly, in time linear in $N_t$. A drifting line keeps a high
score because the path bends to follow it. Broadband power, such as the
continuous-batching floor of the inference null, does not, because no single
slowly varying path stays on top of it. \Cref{fig:viterbi_track} shows both cases on
the contrast map. Averaging over frames makes $V$
comparable across traces of different length. Note that $V$ tests whether a
persistent, slowly wandering line is present, not what produced it. Accordingly, strong lines that do not have a training provenance may also trigger the detector; this is addressed in
\cref{subsec:identifiability}

\begin{figure*}[t]
	\centering
	\includegraphics[width=\linewidth]{viterbi_track}
	\caption{The Viterbi tracker on three $300$\,s traces at the nominal channel.
	Each panel is the contrast map $L_{kj}$ of \cref{eq:contrast} on the
	tracker's own grid ($16$\,s frames at half overlap, $62.5$\,mHz bins over
	$\mathcal{B}$), with the best path of \cref{eq:viterbi} in white and its
	score $V$ inset. Dashed: the true cadence, $1/$(median iteration period)
	in each frame, from the generator's iteration boundaries. Left: a
	stationary training cadence ($f_0 = 0.9$\,Hz), which the path sits on.
	Centre: the same run with $0.4$\,Hz of cadence wander, which the path
	follows across most of the band; it cuts the corner off the brief
	excursion near $150$\,s, where following the line costs more in jumps than
	it gains in contrast. Right: the inference null, where no path finds
	sustained contrast and $V$ falls to $0.73$. Reproduced by
	\texttt{scripts/plot\_viterbi\_track.py}.}
	\label{fig:viterbi_track}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{Setting the threshold}
\label{subsec:threshold}

The tracker declares training when $V$ exceeds a threshold $v_\alpha$, chosen
so that the false-alarm rate is $\alpha$:
\begin{equation}
	\Pr\bigl(V > v_\alpha \mid \mathcal{H}_0\bigr) \;=\; \alpha.
	\label{eq:far}
\end{equation}
We use $\alpha = 10^{-2}$ unless stated. $V$ has no analytic null
distribution. We therefore set $v_\alpha$ empirically, as the
$(1-\alpha)$ quantile of $V$ over simulated traces drawn under
$\mathcal{H}_0$, and measure detection rate as the fraction of $\mathcal{H}_1$
traces above it. The baseline methods of \cref{subsec:comparators} are thresholded
the same way.

In \cref{sec:results} the $\mathcal{H}_0$ population is the null aggregate of
\cref{eq:aggregate_null}. Its background carries the weak lines of the small
trainings and fine-tunings, so the threshold already accounts for any line
that is not the dominant run's. Calibrating on inference alone, with no
background, changes the tracker's detection rates by at most $0.02$
(\cref{app:ceiling}).

This calibrates $V$ against the modelled inference null. A deployed verifier
has to obtain the same threshold from data it holds: from background traces
known to be free of training, as continuous-wave searches set their tracking
thresholds from noise-only realisations \citep{suvorova2016hmm}, or from a
per-trace surrogate, e.g. \cref{app:attribution}. 

\subsection{Baseline method}
\label{subsec:comparators}

Two simple fixed-frequency tests serve as baselines to compare our Viterbi method against. The first is a
spectral matched filter, which uses the peak of the power spectral density in the band,
relative to its median over all frequencies,
\begin{equation}
	D_{\mathrm{MF}} \;=\;
	\frac{\max_{f \in \mathcal{B}} \hat S(f)}{\operatorname{median}_f \hat S(f)},
	\label{eq:matched}
\end{equation}
where $\hat S$ is a Welch estimate of the spectrum of $x[n]$ from half-overlapping
Hann-windowed segments of $1024$ samples ($51.2$\,s at $f_s = 20$\,Hz). The
long segments concentrate a stationary line into one bin, which is the
test's strength; a wandering line smears across many bins and the peak
collapses. The second is the Thomson multitaper harmonic F-test
\citep{thomson1982multitaper,percival1993spectral}, maximised over the band,
\begin{equation}
	D_{\mathrm{F}} \;=\; \max_{f \in \mathcal{B}} F(f),
	\label{eq:ftest}
\end{equation}
where, at any fixed $f$ under a stationary, locally smooth null, $F(f) \sim
F(2, 2K-2)$, with $K = 7$ tapers of time--bandwidth product $NW = 4$. $F(f)$ is the ratio of
the power in a line at $f$ to the power left around it
(\cref{eq:thomson_f}, \cref{app:baselines}). 

% ============================================================================
\section{Detection results}
\label{sec:results}
% ============================================================================

In this section we test the Viterbi tracker of \cref{sec:methods} on synthetic
meter traces. We assess if the Viterbi tracker can detect the training frequency, and what sampling settings are required by the power meter for the Viterbi tracker to work. We treat the operator as benign; an operator who reshapes the schedule
to hide the line is the subject of \cref{sec:frontier}. Under $\mathcal{H}_1$ the meter sees a dominant training run over
$N_{\mathrm{tr}} = 4$ small trainings and $N_{\mathrm{ft}} = 4$ fine-tunings
(\cref{eq:aggregate}). Under $\mathcal{H}_0$ it sees the null aggregate, with
inference in the dominant slot over the same kind of background
(\cref{eq:aggregate_null}). The shares are the defaults of \cref{tab:params},
$9 : 0.5 : 0.5$. Both classes therefore also carry the background's weak lines, and
the tracker has to find the dominant one among them.

This section is organised as follows. \Cref{subsec:power} measures the
tracker's detection rate as the cadence drifts, and compares it with the
fixed-frequency tests of \cref{subsec:comparators} and with an optimality
ceiling. \Cref{subsec:meter_spec} sweeps the meter and states the minimum
specification under which detection holds.

\subsection{Detection rate under cadence wander}
\label{subsec:power}


We consider a range of cadence-drift  $\sigma_f \in \{0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.4, 0.8, 1.5\}$~Hz
(\cref{eq:ou_sigma}) in the dominant training run, with $n=200$ traces of
$300$~s per class and thresholds set at an empirical false-alarm rate of
$10^{-2}$. We benchmark the Viterbi method against a Neyman--Pearson optimal ceiling
(\cref{app:ceiling}). \Cref{fig:drift_ceiling} shows the result. The Viterbi tracker stays within $0.04$ of the optimal ceiling across the
whole $\sigma_f$ axis, with detection rate $1.00$ up to $0.4$~Hz of drift, $0.99$ at
$0.8$~Hz and $0.96$ at $1.5$~Hz. Conversely, the baselines fixed tests struggle. The spectral matched
filter detects a stationary line ($0.98$ at zero drift) but falls to $0.59$ at
$0.1$~Hz and $0.23$ at $0.4$~Hz, and the multitaper F-test has essentially no
power at empirical thresholds at any drift (${\leq}\,0.03$).

%$37$\,dB below the dominant line in power and under the dominant slot's
%broadband floor. Removing the background entirely, and testing a single
%training run against inference alone, changes the tracker's detection rate by
%at most $0.02$ at any drift (\cref{app:ceiling}). The background starts to matter only
%when the dominant share falls. That is the dilution strategy of
%\cref{tab:attacks}, which we take up in \cref{sec:frontier}.

\begin{figure}[t]
	\centering
	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{drift_ceiling_aggregate}
	\caption{Detection rate at empirical false-alarm rate $10^{-2}$ against the
	null aggregate, versus cadence drift $\sigma_f$ of the dominant training run ($n=200$
	per class, $300$~s traces, shares $9 : 0.5 : 0.5$).
	The Viterbi tracker stays within $0.04$ of the Whittle Neyman--Pearson
	ceiling across the wander axis; the spectral matched filter collapses once the line moves and
	the multitaper F-test has no usable power. The ceiling is described in
	\cref{app:ceiling}.}
	\label{fig:drift_ceiling}
\end{figure}

\subsection{A minimum meter specification}
\label{subsec:meter_spec}

The results of \cref{subsec:power} assume the nominal meter of
\cref{tab:meter}: a sample rate of $20$~Hz, no integration window ($\tau \to 0$), no filtering
on the delivery path, and white meter noise of $\sigma_\eta = 4$~W. A real meter
may sample more slowly, average over a longer window, or sit behind a delivery
path that suppresses the cadence band. The meter is the verifier's choice, so it
is of interest to find the minimum specification it must meet for detection to
hold. We sweep the sample rate over $f_s \in \{20, 10, 5, 2, 1, 0.5\}$~Hz and
the integration window over $\tau \in \{0, 0.1, 0.25, 0.5, 1, 2\}$~s
(\cref{eq:boxcar}). We also sweep a notch in the delivery path, i.e. a band near the
cadence in which the delivery path suppresses the power swing
(\cref{subsec:obsmap}). Its centre ranges over $0.6$--$1.2$~Hz and its depth,
the fraction of the signal it removes at the centre, over $50$--$100\%$, with
the meter otherwise nominal. Throughout, the honest aggregate is scored against the null
aggregate, with thresholds at an empirical false-alarm rate of $10^{-2}$ as in
\cref{subsec:power}.

The Viterbi tracker holds full power (detection
rate ${\gtrsim}0.9$) if and only if the meter satisfies three
conditions together (\cref{fig:meter_boundary_viterbi}), one on each part of
\cref{eq:meter}. First, on the sampling, a rate of at least about $2$~Hz: rates of $20$, $10$, $5$, and $2$~Hz all hold the Viterbi tracker
near $1.0$, $1$~Hz collapses it to $0.33$ as the Nyquist edge crosses the band,
and $0.5$~Hz is dead (every detector at chance). Second, on the instrument's
impulse response, an integration window $\tau \lesssim 0.5$~s: at $20$~Hz
sampling $\tau = 0.5$~s still holds ($0.94$), but $\tau = 1$~s puts the first zero
of \cref{eq:boxcar} at $1/\tau = 1$~Hz, the band centre, and collapses the
tracker to $0.32$ even at full sample rate. Third, on the delivery path, no
deep transfer-function notch at the cadence: a shallow notch, or one near the
edge of the cadence band, costs little (tracker ${\geq}0.80$), but a notch of $90$--$100\%$ depth at
$1.0$--$1.2$~Hz roughly halves tracker power (to $0.45$--$0.63$) without erasing
it (\cref{app:meter}).

Against an honest operator, then, detection needs only a meter that samples at
$f_s \geq 2$~Hz, integrates over $\tau \leq 0.5$~s, and has no deep notch at the
cadence.

	\centering
	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{st2_meter_boundary_aggregate_viterbi}
	\caption{Minimum meter specification: Viterbi detection rate at empirical
	false-alarm rate $10^{-2}$ over sample rate $f_s$ $\times$ integration window $\tau$, the
	honest aggregate against the null aggregate ($n=200$ per class). The live region is
	$f_s \ge 2$~Hz \emph{and} $\tau \le 0.5$~s.}

\end{figure}


% ============================================================================
\section{Detection against a concealing operator}
\label{sec:frontier}
% ============================================================================
\Cref{sec:results} assumed a benign operator, who leaves the cadence for the tracker to find. A concealing
operator can instead de-periodicise its schedule and smear the cadence away
(\cref{subsec:adversary}). In principle this is always possible; the concealing operator can insert idle time at random between iterations, or varying the work done in each, to removes any frequency for the Viterbi detector to identify. The question is the cost in training throughput the operator must incur in order de-periodicise enough to hide from the Viterbi detector, and in particular whether any de-periodicisation strategy is both cheap and effective. 


We study four strategies from \cref{tab:attacks}: three timing strategies
(period jitter, work variation and cadence drift) and one waveform strategy
(shape filling). 


We measure the throughput overhead incurred by each strategy on a a single A100.

The operator applies each strategy to its dominant training run on the aggregate
of \cref{sec:results}, the background of small trainings and fine-tunings stays
honest, and every cell is scored against the aggregate null of
\cref{eq:aggregate_null}. 

For each strategy we step its budget knob (\cref{tab:attacks}), which we
call the attack level, over the stated range. At every level we measure the
detection rate of the Viterbi tracker and of the fixed tests of
\cref{subsec:comparators}, taking the better of the two fixed tests at each
cell. All rates are at false-alarm rate $10^{-2}$ with
$n=200$ traces per class. The cost axis is throughput only. A
learning-efficiency penalty, in which an attack keeps tokens per second but
worsens progress per token, cannot be measured in a synthetic model and remains
open (\cref{subsec:scope}). The other four schedule strategies of
\cref{tab:attacks} (phase slip, relocation, harmonic smoothing and dilution) have
no hardware implementation and so no cost. The tracker detects every one of
their cells. The full sweep, these four strategies included, and its
provenance are in \cref{app:sweep}.


We construct the Pareto curve 


To answer it we trace a
Pareto curve : at every throughput cost, the most an operator
can hide at or below that cost. We call this trade-off the de-periodicisation
frontier.



This section is organised as follows. \Cref{subsec:frontier_cost} plots hiding
against measured cost for both detectors, the section's main result.
\Cref{subsec:frontier_costly} shows that the attacks which cost throughput do
not hide the line from the tracker. \Cref{subsec:frontier_work} shows that
varying the real work per iteration hides the line from the fixed tests at no
measurable cost, and that at its strongest level it also halves the tracker's
detection rate, again at no measurable throughput cost. \Cref{subsec:frontier_bound} bounds from below what hiding must
cost, for one adversarial strategy.

\subsection{The cost of hiding}
\label{subsec:frontier_cost}

\Cref{fig:attack_curves} plots hiding ($1-$ detection rate) against measured
throughput overhead for each priced strategy, against the Viterbi tracker
(top) and the fixed tests (bottom). Each line is one strategy's Pareto
staircase: the best hiding that strategy buys at or below a given cost. Against the fixed tests
every strategy hides a lot, but only varying the real work per iteration does so
for free. It hides $0.88$ at zero cost, while jitter and drift need $159\%$ and
$356\%$ overhead to reach $0.88$ and $0.71$. Against the tracker almost every
strategy stays on the floor. Varying the real work is again the exception: at its
strongest level, $0.7$, it hides $0.55$ at zero cost, although at every weaker
level it hides at most $0.05$. Every attack that costs throughput does worse
against the tracker than this free one. The best of them,
idle-insertion jitter at $\sigma_\xi = 0.35$, hides $0.24$ for a $159\%$
overhead. Throughput is therefore not what a concealing operator must pay to
weaken the tracker. Whether the free attack has a price in learning efficiency
instead is the open question of \cref{subsec:frontier_work}.

The drift-free schedule is the honest one, so its cost is zero by
definition.

	\centering

	at false-alarm rate $10^{-2}$ for the Viterbi tracker (solid) and the fixed
	tests (dashed; the better of the matched filter and multitaper F-test per

	shown as $0$; the drift-free schedule is the honest one, so its cost is zero

	are upper bounds. The tracker detects almost every cell. The exception is work
	variation at $\sigma_G = 0.7$, which hides $0.55$ from it at no measurable
	throughput cost; idle-insertion jitter hides at most $0.24$, for $159\%$
	overhead. The meter strategy degrades the channel rather than the schedule
	and is treated in \cref{subsec:meter_spec}. Reproduced by
	\texttt{scripts/plot\_attack\_curves.py}.
	\textcolor{red}{[TODO: figure needs cleaning up before submission.]}}
	\label{fig:attack_curves}
\end{figure*}

\subsection{The costly attacks are the wrong ones}
\label{subsec:frontier_costly}

The de-periodicisations that degrade the line most are exactly the ones a
rational operator would not pay for. Idle-insertion jitter buys little
concealment: it costs $15$--$1027\%$ throughput, and the tracker detects at
least $76\%$ of runs at every level. Slowly drifting the cadence costs
$42$--$2127\%$ and leaves the tracker detecting at least $97\%$ of runs, because
drift is precisely the regime the tracker was built to survive
(\cref{subsec:power}). Power shaping costs
$170$--$230\%$. Against every one of these the tracker holds while the operator
pays a throughput tax that a compute-governance regime would itself flag.
Evasion strategies measured on real hardware are similarly expensive
(\cref{sec:reality}).

\subsection{The free attack: varying real work}
\label{subsec:frontier_work}

The dangerous strategy is variable real work. Varying the useful computation
performed per iteration moves the cadence without inserting idle time, and leaves
the synchronous exchange, which does not shrink with the compute phase,
untouched. Its throughput cost is therefore essentially zero: at work-variation
levels $0.35$, $0.5$ and $0.7$ the measured overhead is $-0.10\%$, $-0.36\%$ and
$-0.65\%$, zero within noise. At that price the fixed tests are gone. The spectral matched
filter falls to detection rate $0.25$ and $0.22$ (its \textsc{auc} collapses to
$0.46$ and $0.43$, below chance), and the multitaper F-test sits at its floor.
Yet the Viterbi tracker holds detection rate $1.0$ and $0.96$. This is the
genuine scope boundary of the passive channel: an operator willing to vary real
work evades every cheap, fixed detector at no measurable systems cost, and up to
level $0.5$ only a tracking detector still sees the schedule. Because the tracker sits near the
Neyman--Pearson ceiling on the honest schedule (\cref{subsec:power}), the gap
reflects information the fixed tests discard, not a well-tuned tracker.

\paragraph{Where the tracker bends, and what it costs.} Pushed to level $0.7$,
the same attack also weakens the tracker: its detection rate falls to $0.46$.
The throughput cost of that level, measured on the same A100 as the other
anchors, is $-0.65\%$, zero within noise. So one strategy halves the tracker's
detection rate at false-alarm rate $10^{-2}$ without costing the operator any
throughput. The mechanism is unsurprising. At level $0.7$ the iteration period
varies by more than its own mean from step to step (cadence coefficient of
variation $1.6$), so the line's power spreads over a band too wide for one
track to collect; and because every micro-step is still real training, the
device never idles.

Two qualifications bound this result. First, the tracker is weakened, not
blinded: it still detects about half of runs, and a longer observation window
may recover more of the spread power. Second, throughput is the only cost we
measure. At level $0.7$ the number of micro-steps accumulated per optimiser step
varies widely, so the effective batch size changes from step to step. Under an
unchanged learning-rate schedule that may slow convergence, in which case the
operator pays in learning efficiency rather than throughput. We have not
measured this (\cref{subsec:scope}). The far end of the frontier is therefore
free in throughput, and its price in learning efficiency is open.

\subsection{A lower bound on the price of hiding}
\label{subsec:frontier_bound}

The frontier bounds hiding
from above: it says what an operator can hide from our detectors, which a better
detector would move. The complementary direction --- what hiding must cost ---
can be argued for one adversarial strategy (\cref{subsec:costbound}). For i.i.d.\
period jitter of scale $\sigma$, no test's detection advantage exceeds the total
variation between the training and null laws, so a verifier that demonstrably
attains advantage $J(\sigma) > \varepsilon$ rules out $\varepsilon$-covertness at
that $\sigma$. With the simplest such verifier, a fixed-bin threshold test at the
nominal cadence, $\varepsilon$-covertness requires $\sigma^{*}(0.5) = 0.18$ and
$\sigma^{*}(0.2) = 0.36$, which the measured anchors price at tens of percent of
throughput and at order $100\%$ respectively. Three limits apply. The bound is
read off the weakest verifier, so it is loose against the tracker, which
\cref{fig:attack_curves} shows to be stronger; it covers one adversarial strategy; and
turning distortion into cost rests on an assumption --- that at fixed useful work,
jitter costs throughput or learning efficiency --- rather than a result.

% ============================================================================
\section{Discussion and conclusion}
\label{sec:discussion}
% ============================================================================

We set out to build a method that turns a low-rate external power trace into a
test for iteration-structured training, to price its evasion against an operator
who knows the test, and to state what the channel cannot certify at any price.
The method is a Viterbi line tracker. Against the inference null that stands for
a facility's declared workload it is essentially Neyman--Pearson optimal across
cadence wander (\cref{subsec:power}), provided the meter samples at ${\geq}2$~Hz
with ${\leq}0.5$~s integration (\cref{subsec:meter_spec}). Varying real work per
iteration evades every fixed-frequency test at no measurable throughput cost.
The tracker survives it until the variation is extreme, where it still detects
about half of runs; that extreme level is also free in throughput, and every
attack that does cost throughput hides less from the tracker
(\cref{sec:frontier}). This section says what such a detection
certifies, where the synthetic evidence stops, and how the result reads for a
regulator.

\subsection{What a detection certifies}
\label{subsec:identifiability}

A detection establishes that the trace carries a training-shaped periodic
schedule. It does not establish that the computation is training. We built
seven control loads whose training status we know and scored them with three
decision rules fitted to separate training from the inference null
(\cref{app:rung2}). Five non-training loads --- a training-shaped non-ML kernel
loop, a controller limit cycle, a periodic inference request generator, a
gradient-only computation, and a discarded-update decoy that runs the full
forward, backward and optimiser step and throws the update away --- all score as
training under every rule (\cref{tab:rung2_controls}).

The adversary operators of \cref{subsec:adversary} deliberately omit the
extremal member of this class. A \emph{semantic decoy} --- a load reproducing the physical schedule of training
without retaining a trained model --- is not an attack a concealing operator would
mount, since manufacturing evidence of the activity it is hiding buys it nothing.
It enters this paper instead as a non-training control
(\cref{tab:rung2_controls}) and as the construction behind the
non-identifiability argument below, and it carries weight for two
reasons that need no motivated decoy-runner: its benign counterparts occur in
ordinary datacentre operation, and the active protocol of \cref{app:active}
inverts the operator's objective, at which point a \emph{challenge-aware decoy} ---
a correlated dummy response mimicking the prescribed reaction without training ---
does become a live attack.

The ceiling is a property of the channel, not of our classifiers. Write $w$ for a computational execution, $h$ for the hardware and
power-delivery path, and $K_h(w)$ for the law of the observed trace that
\cref{eq:meter} induces. Call two executions \emph{observationally
equivalent} when $K_{h_0}(w_0) = K_{h_1}(w_1)$. A passive verifier sees only the
trace, so its decision is some measurable function of it, and on an
observationally equivalent pair every such function fires with the same
probability under both. No passive scalar-power detector can therefore certify
the semantic content of a computation against an unrestricted adversary. A
non-vacuous guarantee has to put the equivalent pairs out of scope, and there are
four ways to do that within the passive channel --- restricting the admissible
non-training workload class, the adversary's freedom to add or restructure
computation, the hardware and power-transfer family, or the physical property
claimed --- alongside a fifth route that leaves the passive channel altogether by
changing the protocol (\cref{app:active}). We do not claim the list is exhaustive.

The construction behind this is nearly available on the operator's own hardware. A
program can execute the same forward, backward, and optimiser kernels as training
and discard each updated state, making its trace arbitrarily close to genuine
training while its semantic classification differs. This is not a hypothetical
weakness; it is what \cref{tab:rung2_controls} measures. That outcome is a
property of the channel rather than of our classifiers, which is why this ceiling
cannot be removed by a better detector and why escaping it requires an active
challenge (\cref{app:active}).

The argument binds even where no adversary is present. A concealing operator has no
reason to run a decoy (\cref{subsec:adversary}), but most of the equivalence class
is not adversarial at all: a training-shaped non-ML kernel loop, a controller
limit cycle, and a periodic inference request generator all sit inside it, and all
arise in ordinary operation. The consequence is two-sided. A rule phrased
semantically --- training rather than serving, which model, whose weights ---
cannot be adjudicated from the schedule alone in either direction, so the same
equivalence that would let a decoy counterfeit training also caps the evidentiary
weight a verifier can attach to a positive detection.

\paragraph{Instrument lines and false alarms.} The same reading covers the
tracker's one systematic failure. A periodic physical confound, such as the
power-controller oscillation measured on an A100 (\cref{sec:reality}), is a
persistent wandering line, and the Viterbi score cannot tell it from training
(\cref{subsec:confound}). The failure matters for honest operators rather than
concealing ones: a controller line does not help an operator hide training, but it
can flag a compliant inference facility. Three things bound it. First, a
known-line veto. Continuous-wave searches meet the same problem in instrumental
lines, and handle it by cataloguing lines from detector characterisation data
and discarding candidates coincident with them.
% TODO(cite): a LIGO known-lines / line-veto reference, e.g. Covas et al. 2018,
% PRD 97, 082002 -- verify with /check-refs before adding to references.bib.
The analogue here is to extract several candidate paths from the contrast map
(\cref{eq:contrast}) and discard those that coincide with lines catalogued from
the facility's own characterisation data. We have not evaluated it, and it carries a cost a gravitational-wave veto does not: the
adversary knows the veto list, and can relocate its cadence into a vetoed band.
Second, per-card controllers need not add coherently at a facility meter
(\cref{sec:reality}). Third, a positive detection is a trigger for escalation
rather than a verdict, and the active protocol of \cref{app:active} resolves a
controller false alarm as it resolves the decoys above. The order-tracked
cyclostationary statistic of \cref{app:attribution} partly separates the
modelled controller from training by waveform shape, but only conditionally, and
we do not rely on it.

% ============================================================================
\subsection{Reality check and transfer limits}
\label{sec:reality}
% ============================================================================

Every result above is synthetic. The one place we hold the scenario model
against measured hardware, it fails in an instructive way, and we report that
failure as a result rather than a closing nod.

\paragraph{The negative transport case.} On measured single-A100 traces the
iteration cadence is present but shallow: a saturated card has no communication
phase, so the iteration structure modulates a ${\sim}370$\,W draw by only a few
watts (${\sim}0.4\%$ of board power). Worse for the naive reading, the spectra
contain a $0.31$--$0.45$\,Hz component, roughly ten times stronger than the
training line, that appears whenever the load varies in time but not at idle or
under constant load --- the signature of the card's own power-management loop. It
is a hardware line that says ``time-varying load,'' not ``training,'' and it is
the instrument line of \cref{subsec:identifiability}: the standing
counterexample to reading any detected line as training.

\paragraph{Why this is the honest outcome.} Two things make the single-card
signature shallow. One saturated card has no synchronous communication barrier,
so the deep compute--communication contrast the scenario model assumes is absent;
and the generator is literature-parameterised, not calibrated to the measured
channel, a gap of about $75\times$ in modulation depth. The synthetic results are
therefore a sensitivity analysis over a plausible parameter family, not a
prediction calibrated to this hardware --- which is why the paper's claims are
scoped to the stated generator and its stated nulls throughout.

\paragraph{The single-card gap is shared, and lands differently.} The measured
side-channel corpus that separates training from inference at high bandwidth is
also a single card, with cross-device generalisation left open
\citep{gargiulo2026workload}. What differs is which observable the gap touches. A
board-level probe reads the optimizer-update phase, which is present on one card,
so the absent distributed setting costs that result little. The cadence is a
collective effect of synchronisation, so a single card is exactly the case in
which it is weakest --- which is why the same gap is a transport caveat there and a
first-order limitation here. The two results also bound each other. The probe's
signature sits below about $20$~kHz and survives decimation to about $38$~kS/s,
three to four orders of magnitude above the few hertz our specification needs,
so the fine structure a probe exploits is gone by the time a facility meter
reads, and whatever survives at a few hertz must be a slower, more collective
observable.

\paragraph{Measured evasion costs agree.} Work on real hardware prices
de-periodicisation the same way as our anchors, through a different channel. Four
evasion strategies run on a single H200 --- chunked optimizer updates, dilution
with decoy inference, throttling, and diluted LoRA --- cost between $28$ and
$69\%$ of throughput \citep{gargiulo2026workload}. Each inserts or substitutes
work, which is what makes it expensive, and none varies the real computation per
iteration, the one strategy \cref{subsec:frontier_work} finds cheap.

\paragraph{Falsifiable predictions.} The model makes three predictions we cannot
test here but state as falsifiable. Distributed synchronisation should deepen the
line: at cluster scale the periodic all-reduce barrier produces a deep, coherent,
legible cadence rather than the shallow single-card ripple, which is precisely the
physics the cost-of-hiding assumption leans on. And an
external wall or rack meter should see a different, lower-passed trace than
on-board NVML telemetry, shifting where the minimum meter specification of
\cref{subsec:meter_spec} binds. And per-card power-controller oscillations,
which dominate the single-card spectrum, should add incoherently across a
cluster --- roughly as $\sqrt{N}$ for $N$ independent controllers, against $N$
for a synchronous training line --- and so fall relative to the training line at
a facility meter. All three are predictions, not results.

\subsection{The claim ladder}
\label{subsec:ladder}

The results can be read back as a \emph{claim ladder} (\cref{tab:ladder}): four
claims of increasing governance relevance, each bought at a stated cost in
verifier information, and each with a hard ceiling that motivates the next.
Read as a procedure, it is screening followed by escalation. Rung~1 establishes
that coherent periodic power structure is present, which is evidence rather than
identification. Rung~2 converts that structure into training-likeness at the
price of committing to an inference null; the detection results of this paper
live here, and its ceiling is semantic non-identifiability. Rungs~3 and~4 leave
the passive channel for an active protocol and a transcript primitive, and are
specified but not run (\cref{app:active}). The ladder is a ladder of claims and
assumptions, not a quantitative bound on unidentified compute.

\subsection{Scope, limitations, and governance reading}
\label{subsec:scope}

\paragraph{Scope.} Three restrictions fix what the results cover. First, the
observable: we use the time-resolved power trace and exclude the
integrated-energy channel, so there is no bounding of how much compute was
performed and no energy-per-token pricing as a verification instrument. This is
a restriction on the observable, not a claim that everything lives in the
spectrum; cyclostationary structure is expressed spectrally, but the challenge
correlation of the active protocol is a time-domain operation on the same trace. Second, the
population: we do not claim a recoverable cadence is universally necessary for
training, and some conceivable execution can be made fully aperiodic. We target
efficient, synchronous, iteration-structured training that exposes a recoverable
cadence, the expected physical signature of that regime where distributed
synchronisation makes the modulation deep and coherent. Destroying that cadence
is then an adversarial action with a measurable budget, not a counterexample to
the method, and measuring that budget is what \cref{sec:frontier} does. The
declared workload need not be pure inference either: a facility may be permitted
fine-tuning or training below a threshold, whose lines our detector would also
find, and telling which line and how large a run it represents needs the
integrated-energy channel we exclude. Third,
the horizon: the results are fixed-horizon, and we make no claim that our
statistics support anytime-valid monitoring, deferring sequential
e-process treatment. The cryptographic binding of the active protocol is assumed as an ideal
functionality, not built. Real distributed hardware enters only as the
falsifiable predictions and the negative transport case of \cref{sec:reality}.

\paragraph{Limitations.} The scenario model is literature-parameterised, not
calibrated to measured hardware, so every quantitative result is a sensitivity
analysis over a stated parameter family; the ${\sim}75\times$ modulation gap of
\cref{sec:reality} is the standing reminder. The observation map is a
linear time-invariant first approximation. The optimality ceiling of
\cref{app:ceiling} is optimal only under the Whittle model, hence a lower bound on
the true optimum. Every robustness claim is bounded by the adversarial strategies
and budgets we specified; a strategy we did not model is outside it. The most
important such strategy is energy storage between the accelerators and the
meter. A store sized to the cadence swing can discharge during each compute
phase and recharge during each communication phase, so that the meter sees a
flat load. This costs the operator no throughput, so our frontier cannot price
it; its costs are converters rated for the full swing, wear from cycling at
the cadence, and conversion losses. Power smoothing of this kind is a grid
mitigation for training load in its own right \citep{ko2025widearea}, so it
may be installed for reasons unrelated to concealment. The verifier's remedy
is placement: a meter between any storage and the accelerators sees the
unsmoothed load. The cost bound of
\cref{subsec:costbound} shares that limit: it covers i.i.d.\ period jitter,
and while it holds against any verifier class containing the test it exhibits, it is
obtained from a fixed-bin test and so reads loose against the Viterbi tracker our own
experiments show to be stronger --- it does not yet close the frontier's far end. Its cost leg is an
assumption, not a result, for the reasons set out in
\cref{subsec:costbound}. The tracker's thresholds are calibrated by Monte Carlo on
the modelled null, not per trace, and the known-line veto that would handle
instrument lines is specified but not evaluated. And the learning-efficiency leg of that bound --- the axis that would
turn it into a single priced statement rather than a disjunction --- is argued,
not measured, and remains the central open empirical question. It now matters
directly: the one attack that weakens the tracker is free in throughput, so
learning efficiency is the only place it could be paid for.

\paragraph{Governance reading.} What a regulator can buy today is a screen. From
an external meter alone, meeting the specification of \cref{subsec:meter_spec}, a
Viterbi tracker detects the iteration cadence of synchronous training against a
declared inference workload, robust to cadence wander, drift, and moderate
variable-work evasion, which already defeats every fixed-frequency test. Extreme
variable work halves its detection rate at no throughput cost; whether that
attack costs learning efficiency is untested.
It does not certify that the computation is training rather than a
schedule-matched mimic, benign or deliberate, and it cannot by itself tell
training from a periodic instrument line. Both are limits of the passive
channel, not of the method, and they run both ways: they cap what a positive
detection proves as well as what a counterfeit could fake. A positive detection
should therefore trigger escalation --- to the active protocol of
\cref{app:active} and the cryptographic primitive it assumes --- rather than stand
as proof of training. The passive meter is a cheap, deployable front line that
narrows the question and prices the cheap evasions.
